turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Reddy, I'm Sister Dlamini. Before the doctor calls you, your blood pressure is 118 over 72, pulse 88, temperature 36.8, oxygen saturation 98 percent, and your respiratory rate is 16.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Sister. I appreciate you doing that so promptly.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good morning, Mrs Reddy. I'm Dr Pillay. Sister mentioned bleeding in early pregnancy, but I'd rather hear it from you. What's been going on?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. I believe I am pregnant, perhaps eight to ten weeks, though I may be wrong about that, and I have had some spotting with cramping low down. I am rather anxious about it.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can hear that you're worried, and we'll go step by step. When was your last period?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, the last period was around Diwali, or after. I did not write the date down, so I cannot be more precise than that.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, so the dates are soft, and I won't pin a gestation on that today. How much blood are you losing, a pad or only when you wipe?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I have been very careful at school, Doctor. I teach grade four, and I did not want the children to see that I was unwell, so I have been sitting down more than I usually would.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's fair enough, but I do still need the amount. Are you soaking a pad, or is it only a smear?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Only a smear, Doctor. It is brown, mostly, on a pantyliner, and I have not soaked anything. It has been about a week.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the cramps, where exactly, and how bad are they?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Low, across the middle, a dull ache. It comes and goes, and I would call it mild. It began a few days after the spotting, if I am remembering correctly.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any pain just on one side, left or right?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose... sometimes, not really. It is difficult to be sure.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right, I won't take that as a yes. Any dizziness, or did you actually faint?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt a little light-headed once, yesterday, when I stood up quickly. I did not faint.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, burning when you pass urine, or an unusual discharge?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none of those. My waterworks have been quite normal.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): And shortness of breath, or chest pain?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. Nothing like that.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you taking any medicines at the moment?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I take folic acid, by mouth, once a day. I think the dose is five milligrams, though I have not looked at the bottle this week. There is also a small white tablet my GP gave me for nausea, and I cannot remember the name.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): How often do you take that white tablet?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Only when the nausea is troublesome, not every day. I have missed the folic acid on a few mornings as well, so I am not certain I have taken it as I should.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the nausea still with you?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, a mild queasiness most mornings. No vomiting.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I am aware of, Doctor. I have no known allergies.
[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, her husband has been waiting outside, and he asked if he may come in. Shall I fetch him?
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please do, Sister. Mrs Reddy, are you happy for him to join us?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, that would be quite all right. Thank you.
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): I'll bring him through just now.
[SEG0033] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, the parking was a proper mission. I'm Kuben, her husband. She's been bleeding quite heavily, Doctor, changing pads, and it's been two weeks, not a few days.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, that is not correct. It is only spotting, and I have not filled a pad. It has been about a week, not two.
[SEG0035] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she nearly blacked out yesterday in the kitchen. I had to sit her down.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I did not black out. I was light-headed for a moment, as I told you, and I remained standing.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you both. I won't smooth that over. We'll treat the bleeding as spotting that may have gone on somewhere between a week and two weeks, and the faint as not agreed.
[SEG0038] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She also swelled up with penicillin when she was small. Her face puffed, and we've avoided it since.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): That was my sister, not me. I have never had penicillin, and I do not have allergies.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The folic acid bottle at home says 400 micrograms, one tablet a day. Not five milligrams.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I was told five milligrams at the clinic. Well, actually, perhaps there are two bottles, and I am not sure which one I have been taking.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the folic acid dose is not settled, and we'll leave the white tablet unnamed until you bring the box. Don't start anything new, and don't stop the folate.

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud for a moment, rather than jump. Spotting with cramps at this stage can be a threatened miscarriage, and it can also be something benign, like bleeding from the cervix. I cannot rule out an ectopic pregnancy, especially with these soft dates and that unclear one-sided story, and I am not going to conclude any of those today, because the scan and the bloods have to speak first.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll examine your abdomen now, if that's all right. Just lie back.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Of course, Doctor.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): The abdomen is soft. There is mild tenderness low down in the middle, no guarding and no rebound. I can't feel the uterus from the outside, which I'd expect this early, so I'll leave the internal examination for the scan room rather than put you through it twice.

[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): The plan for today is a pelvic ultrasound, to see where the pregnancy is and to check the dates, plus bloods: a pregnancy hormone, your blood group and rhesus, and a full blood count. Sister will send the bloods this morning, and the scan is booked for this afternoon downstairs.
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): I can take her for the bloods as soon as you're finished, and reception has held the scan for two o'clock.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Please keep taking whichever folate you have been on, one tablet a day, until we sort the strength. Bring both bottles next time, and the box for that white tablet.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall do that.

[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): No intercourse, and take it easy, until we have seen the scan. If the bleeding becomes heavier than a pantyliner, if the pain turns severe, if you get shoulder pain, or if you feel you might faint, come straight back to casualty. Do not wait until morning.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I will come immediately if any of that happens.
[SEG0053] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring her, Doctor. We won't sit on it.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd also like to see you back in two days with the results, regardless, so we can talk the scan through properly.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days is manageable. I can arrange cover at school.

[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): The other thing I will not decide today is hormone treatment. Some clinicians use progesterone for spotting, but I do not have a reason to start it before we know where the pregnancy is sitting.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): I would prefer not to take anything extra unless it is necessary.
[SEG0058] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's hardly slept, Doctor. She's been up half the night worrying.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I have been anxious, yes, but I did sleep a few hours. It is not quite as he describes.

[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): The worry is understandable, and we'll have more to say once the scan is done. Sister, bloods first, then she can wait for the scan. Any heavy bleeding before then is casualty, not the waiting room.
[SEG0061] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you to the blood room now, Mrs Reddy. Bring your husband. If you feel faint on the way, we stop and call the doctor.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Sister. Thank you, Doctor. I am grateful you have laid it out so clearly.

spec.situation: Woman about 8-10 weeks pregnant with spotting and cramps; unsure of dates ('the last period was around Diwali, or after'); anxious; partner waits outside then joins. Scan and blood tests planned today, strict return advice.
features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Urgent return to casualty is advised, not a follow-up consultation.
bad.text: Follow-up consultation (action_type=follow_up, status=conditional, responsible_person=doctor, time_reference=value: if the bleeding becomes heavier than a pantyliner, if the pain turns severe, if you get shoulder pain, or if you feel you might faint)

omissions.text: Vaginal spotting was described as brown, mostly seen on a pantyliner, and the patient specifically said she had not soaked anything/filled a pad.
Cramping pain was low across the middle and dull in character.
Possible one-sided pain was specifically asked about and not confirmed: the patient was unsure and the doctor said he would not take that as a yes.
The patient denied fainting/syncope when asked directly ('I did not faint').
The patient reported normal urination/'waterworks have been quite normal.'
Folic acid dose was mentioned by the patient as 'I think 5 milligrams' before later becoming disputed/uncertain.
The patient reported she has missed folic acid on a few mornings and is not sure she has taken it as she should.
No known allergies was stated by the patient as 'Not that I am aware of, Doctor. I have no known allergies.'
Internal examination was deferred: the doctor said he would leave the internal examination for the scan room rather than put her through it twice.
Timing/details of investigations were given: bloods were to be sent that morning and the pelvic ultrasound was booked for that afternoon/downstairs, with reception holding the scan for 2 o'clock.

Return precautions included coming straight back to casualty and not waiting until morning if bleeding became heavier than a pantyliner, pain became severe, shoulder pain developed, or she felt she might faint.
The doctor additionally told staff/patient that any heavy bleeding before the scan should be managed in casualty, not the waiting room.
The doctor stated he would not decide on hormone treatment today and specifically would not start progesterone before knowing where the pregnancy is located.
